title: German B1
description: The third step in German, from A2 to CEFR level B1, the level of the Goethe-Zertifikat B1. Lessons cover telling stories in the simple past and past perfect, time clauses, the future, weak and adjectival nouns, obwohl, um … zu and damit, two-part connectors, relative clauses in every case, the genitive, the passive, the full Konjunktiv II, verbs with prepositions, and writing e-mails, forum posts and short presentations. About 1,000 new words build on the 1,384 from German A1 and A2 for about 2,400 in all, and a reading list suggests graded readers and real news at this level. Unlocks when German A2 is complete.
author: Examiner

modules.title: If only: Konjunktiv II and more
Living independently and the B1 exam

lessons.title: Telling stories: the simple past
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

At A2 you learned to *recognise* the **[[simple past]]** (*Präteritum*) in stories: *ging, kam, sah, fand*. You also learned to *use* it for *sein, haben, werden* and the modal verbs. At B1 that is not enough. You read novels, news and biographies, and you are expected to write a short story or a report yourself. Those texts are written in the simple past, so now you learn to produce it for every kind of verb.

This lesson brings together the three verb types, shows you the vowel patterns that make the strong verbs much easier to learn, explains what happens to separable verbs, and tells you when Germans write *sie fuhr* and when they say *sie ist gefahren*. The theme is stories: novels, heroes, authors, events and a small mystery.

## The endings: one set for every verb

All verbs share the same personal endings in the simple past. The *ich* and *er/sie/es* forms have no ending at all.

| | ending | weak: sagen | strong: finden | mixed: denken |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ich | – | sagte | fand | dachte |
| du | -st | sagtest | fandest | dachtest |
| er / sie / es | – | sagte | fand | dachte |
| wir | -en / -n | sagten | fanden | dachten |
| ihr | -t | sagtet | fandet | dachtet |
| sie / Sie | -en / -n | sagten | fanden | dachten |

So the whole job is finding the **[[past stem]]**: *sagte-*, *fand-*, *dachte-*. Once you have it, the endings are automatic. (A strong stem ending in *-d* or *-t* adds an *-e-* before *-st* and *-t* for easier pronunciation: *du fandest, ihr fandet*. You will rarely need these forms, because the *du* and *ihr* forms almost only appear in speech, where people use the perfect.)

## Weak verbs: stem + -te

A **[[weak verb]]** keeps its vowel and adds *-te*: *machen → machte, kaufen → kaufte, berichten → berichtete*. Stems ending in *-t*, *-d* or certain consonant clusters add *-ete* so you can hear the ending: *arbeiten → arbeitete, gründen → gründete, öffnen → öffnete*.

Verbs in *-ieren* are weak too: *studierte, passierte, telefonierte*. Inseparable prefixes stay on: *entdecken → entdeckte, veröffentlichen → veröffentlichte, erzählen → erzählte*.

- *Die Zeitung berichtete über das Ereignis.* — The newspaper reported on the event.
- *Ein Bauer entdeckte die Höhle im Jahr 1923.* — A farmer discovered the cave in 1923.
- *Die Autorin veröffentlichte ihren ersten Roman mit 24.* — The author published her first novel at 24.

## Strong verbs: a new vowel, no -te

A **[[strong verb]]** changes its stem vowel and takes no *-te*: *finden → fand, schreiben → schrieb, fahren → fuhr*. You have to learn each one, but you do not have to learn them as 150 separate facts. Most follow a handful of vowel patterns (in German grammar this vowel change is called **[[ablaut]]**). Learn the pattern with one model verb, and the others fall into place.

| pattern | model | Präteritum | Perfekt | other verbs like it |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ei → ie → ie | schreiben | schrieb | hat geschrieben | bleiben, scheinen, steigen, leihen |
| ei → i → i | schneiden | schnitt | hat geschnitten | reiten (ritt), streiten (stritt), leiden (litt) |
| ie → o → o | fliegen | flog | ist geflogen | verlieren, schieben, fliehen (floh) |
| i → a → u | finden | fand | hat gefunden | trinken, singen, springen, verschwinden |
| i → a → o | beginnen | begann | hat begonnen | schwimmen, gewinnen |
| e → a → o | sprechen | sprach | hat gesprochen | helfen, nehmen, treffen, sterben, stehlen |
| e → a → e | geben | gab | hat gegeben | lesen, sehen, essen (aß), vergessen, geschehen |
| a → u → a | fahren | fuhr | ist gefahren | tragen, schlagen, waschen, einladen (lud ein) |
| a → ie → a | schlafen | schlief | hat geschlafen | fallen (fiel), halten (hielt), lassen (ließ) |

A few common verbs follow no pattern and are simply irregular: *gehen → ging*, *stehen → stand*, *kommen → kam*, *sitzen → saß*, *liegen → lag*, *tun → tat*, *rufen → rief*, *laufen → lief*, *heißen → hieß*. The reference sheet at the end of the module lists about seventy verbs grouped like this.

Two memory hooks help:

- **The *ich* form equals the *er* form.** *Ich fand, er fand. Ich schrieb, sie schrieb.* No *-e*, no *-t*. A form like ~~er fande~~ or ~~ich schriebte~~ is never right.
- **Many common *ei* verbs are strong**, and when they are, they go to *ie* or *i*: *bleiben – blieb, scheinen – schien, schneiden – schnitt*. But some everyday *ei* verbs are weak, so check new ones: *arbeiten, heiraten, meinen, reisen, teilen, zeigen*.

Examples from stories:

- *Plötzlich verschwand der Ring.* — Suddenly the ring disappeared.
- *Der Held sprang ins Wasser und schwamm zum Ufer.* — The hero jumped into the water and swam to the shore.
- *Niemand wusste, was in der Nacht geschehen war.* — Nobody knew what had happened in the night.
- *Der Dieb stahl die Krone und floh durch den Garten.* — The thief stole the crown and fled through the garden.

## Mixed verbs: a new vowel and -te

A small group, the **[[mixed verbs]]**, does both: the vowel changes like a strong verb, and *-te* is added like a weak one. There are only about eight you need, and you know their participles already from A2 (*gebracht, gedacht, gekannt*).

| infinitive | Präteritum | Perfekt |
|---|---|---|
| bringen | brachte | hat gebracht |
| denken | dachte | hat gedacht |
| kennen | kannte | hat gekannt |
| nennen | nannte | hat genannt |
| rennen | rannte | ist gerannt |
| wissen | wusste | hat gewusst |
| brennen | brannte | hat gebrannt |
| senden | sandte / sendete | hat gesandt / gesendet |

*Er kannte die Antwort, aber er nannte keinen Namen.* — He knew the answer, but he didn't give a name.

## Separable verbs in the simple past

In a main clause a **[[separable verb]]** splits in the simple past exactly as it does in the present: the past form goes to position 2, the prefix to the end.

- present: *Sie steht um sechs auf.*
- simple past: *Sie stand um sechs auf.* — She got up at six.
- *Der Zug kam pünktlich an.* — The train arrived on time.
- *Er rief sofort die Polizei an.* — He phoned the police at once.

In a subordinate clause the verb goes to the end and joins up again: *…, als sie um sechs aufstand*; *…, weil der Zug pünktlich ankam*. This is the same rule you know from the present.

## Written past, spoken past

Both past tenses mean the same thing. The choice depends on the kind of text:

| | simple past (Präteritum) | perfect (Perfekt) |
|---|---|---|
| typical texts | novels, fairy tales, news reports, biographies, history books, formal reports | conversation, chats, informal e-mails and letters |
| verbs | all verbs | most verbs (but *war, hatte*, modals in the simple past) |
| feel | narrative, distant, finished | personal, connected to now |

A newspaper writes *Der Bürgermeister eröffnete gestern die neue Brücke*; a friend tells you *Gestern hat der Bürgermeister die neue Brücke eröffnet*. Same fact, different register.

There is also a regional difference. In northern Germany the simple past is quite common in speech, even for verbs like *ging* and *kam*: *Ich kam gestern nach Hause und …*. In southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland, everyday speech uses almost only the perfect; Swiss German dialects have lost the simple past almost completely. In writing, everyone uses the simple past for stories. For you this means: write stories and reports in the simple past, but in conversation, use the perfect for most verbs.

## Story words: telling a story in order

Stories need words that move the action forward. Some you know (*zuerst, dann, danach, plötzlich, am Ende*). New at B1:

| word | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *eines Tages* | one day | *Eines Tages kam ein Brief aus Amerika.* |
| *zunächst* | at first, initially | *Zunächst glaubte ihr niemand.* |
| *schließlich* | in the end, eventually | *Schließlich fand die Polizei den Dieb.* |
| *im Verlauf* (+ genitive or *von*) | in the course of | *Im Verlauf des Abends wurde es kalt.* |
| *am Ende* | at the end | *Am Ende heirateten der Held und die Heldin.* |

*Eines Tages* is a fixed phrase in the genitive; use it like *an einem Tag*. It opens the story's main event, just like English "one day".

## Text: Das verschwundene Manuskript

> Im Frühling 1987 geschah in einer kleinen Stadt am Bodensee etwas Seltsames. Die ehemalige Lehrerin Margarete Vogt hatte ihr ganzes Leben lang heimlich geschrieben, aber nie etwas veröffentlicht. Eines Tages schickte sie das Manuskript ihres ersten Romans an einen Verlag in München. Die Handlung spielte in ihrer eigenen Stadt, und die Heldin war eine junge Postbotin, die alle Geheimnisse der Nachbarn kannte.
>
> Zwei Wochen später kam ein Brief: Der Verlag wollte das Buch drucken. Doch am nächsten Morgen war das Manuskript aus ihrem Schreibtisch verschwunden. Frau Vogt rief sofort die Polizei an. Ein Nachbar erzählte, er habe nachts ein Licht im Garten gesehen, aber er war kein guter Zeuge, denn er trug keine Brille.
>
> Zunächst fand die Polizei keine Spur. Dann bemerkte ein junger Polizist etwas: Einige Figuren im Roman sahen den Nachbarn sehr ähnlich, und nicht alle kamen gut weg. Schließlich gab der Bäcker von gegenüber zu, dass er das Manuskript gestohlen hatte. Er hatte sich im dritten Kapitel wiedererkannt und schämte sich.
>
> Das Buch erschien im Herbst. Am Ende des Romans stand ein neuer Satz: „Alle Figuren sind frei erfunden.“ Die Leser glaubten es natürlich nicht.

Translation:

> In the spring of 1987 something strange happened in a small town on Lake Constance. The former teacher Margarete Vogt had secretly written all her life but had never published anything. One day she sent the manuscript of her first novel to a publisher in Munich. The plot was set in her own town, and the heroine was a young postwoman who knew all the neighbours' secrets.
>
> Two weeks later a letter came: the publisher wanted to print the book. But the next morning the manuscript had disappeared from her desk. Mrs Vogt phoned the police at once. A neighbour said he had seen a light in the garden at night, but he was not a good witness, because he wasn't wearing his glasses.
>
> At first the police found no trace. Then a young policeman noticed something: some characters in the novel looked very similar to the neighbours, and not all of them came off well. In the end the baker from across the road admitted that he had stolen the manuscript. He had recognised himself in the third chapter and was ashamed.
>
> The book came out in the autumn. At the end of the novel there was a new sentence: "All characters are entirely fictional." The readers didn't believe it, of course.

Notes: almost every verb is in the simple past, as in any written story. Weak: *schickte, wollte, erzählte, bemerkte, schämte sich, glaubten*. Strong: *geschah, kam, war, trug, fand, sahen, gab … zu, erschien, stand*. Mixed: *kannte*. Separable: *rief … an, gab … zu*. *hatte geschrieben, war verschwunden, gestohlen hatte* are the past perfect, the topic of the next lesson. *er habe … gesehen* is reported speech, which you only need to recognise for now. *der Verlag* = publishing house; *heimlich* = secretly; *das Geheimnis* = secret; *gut wegkommen* = to come off well; *zugeben* (gab zu) = to admit; *frei erfunden* = entirely made up.

## Pronunciation

- *geschah*: ge-SCHAH, a long *a*. The present is *es geschieht*.
- *der Held*: the *d* at the end sounds like *t*: [hɛlt]. Plural *die Helden*: HEL-den.
- *erschien*: er-SCHIEN, long *ie*; *verschwand*: ver-SCHWANT.
- *die Biografie*: stress on the last syllable, bi-o-gra-FIE. The same for *die Fantasie*: fan-ta-SIE.
- *das Kapitel*: ka-PI-tel, stress on the second syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Adding *-te* to a strong verb: ~~er fandte~~, ~~sie gingte~~ → *er fand, sie ging*.
- Adding an ending to the *ich* or *er* form: ~~er kame~~, ~~ich sahe~~ → *er kam, ich sah*.
- Mixing up the vowel with the participle: the past of *finden* is *fand*, not ~~fund~~ (*gefunden* is the participle); the past of *sprechen* is *sprach*, not ~~sproch~~.
- Not separating the prefix in a main clause: ~~Sie aufstand um sechs~~ → *Sie stand um sechs auf.*
- Forgetting the *-e-* in weak verbs in *-t*/*-d*: ~~er arbeitte~~, ~~sie berichtte~~ → *er arbeitete, sie berichtete*.
- Writing a whole conversation in the simple past. *Ich ging gestern ins Kino und sah einen Film* is fine in a story but sounds bookish in a chat with a friend in southern Germany; say *Ich bin gestern ins Kino gegangen*.

## Key points

- Every verb uses the same endings in the simple past: *ich –, du -st, er –, wir -en, ihr -t, sie -en*. The *ich* and *er* forms are identical.
- Weak verbs: stem + *-te* (*sagte*), or *-ete* after *-t/-d* (*berichtete*).
- Strong verbs: new vowel, no *-te* (*fand, schrieb, fuhr*). Learn them in vowel-pattern groups.
- Mixed verbs: new vowel + *-te* (*brachte, dachte, kannte, wusste*).
- Separable verbs split in main clauses: *Sie stand auf. Er rief an.*
- Write stories, reports and biographies in the simple past; speak mostly in the perfect, especially in the south.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Before that: the past perfect, nachdem and bevor
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In the last lesson's story, the manuscript *war verschwunden* and the baker *hatte* it *gestohlen*. Those forms take you one step further back: they describe something that happened *before* another past event. This is the **[[past perfect]]** (*Plusquamperfekt*), English "had done".

The past perfect matters most with *nachdem* (after), which almost always needs it, and it makes your stories clearer: the reader knows what happened first without extra words. This lesson also covers *bevor* (before), the rules for which tense goes with which, and the time adverbs *vorher, zuvor* and *anschließend*. The theme is history: wars, the Berlin Wall, the *Wende* of 1989 and the people who lived through it.

## The form: hatte or war + participle

The past perfect is built exactly like the perfect, but the helper verb is in the simple past: *hatte* instead of *hat*, *war* instead of *ist*. Anything that takes *haben* in the perfect takes *hatte* here; anything with *sein* takes *war*.

| | with haben | with sein |
|---|---|---|
| ich | hatte … gesehen | war … geflohen |
| du | hattest … gesehen | warst … geflohen |
| er / sie / es | hatte … gesehen | war … geflohen |
| wir | hatten … gesehen | waren … geflohen |
| ihr | hattet … gesehen | wart … geflohen |
| sie / Sie | hatten … gesehen | waren … geflohen |

- perfect: *Die Familie ist 1961 nach Westberlin geflohen.*
- past perfect: *Die Familie war 1961 nach Westberlin geflohen.* — The family had fled to West Berlin in 1961.
- perfect: *Der Krieg hat die Stadt zerstört.*
- past perfect: *Der Krieg hatte die Stadt zerstört.* — The war had destroyed the city.

Word order is the same as in the perfect: the helper in position 2, the participle at the end (the sentence bracket); in a subordinate clause the helper goes to the very end: *…, weil der Krieg die Stadt zerstört hatte.*

There is nothing new to learn about participles. If you know *ist geflohen*, you know *war geflohen*.

## When to use it

Use the past perfect for an event that was already finished *before* the time you are talking about in the past. Think of two points on a timeline: your story is at point B (simple past or perfect), and you look back to point A (past perfect).

- *Als wir am Bahnhof ankamen, war der Zug schon abgefahren.* — When we got to the station, the train had already left. (The train left first.)
- *Sie konnte nicht mitkommen. Sie hatte sich das Bein gebrochen.* — She couldn't come. She had broken her leg.
- *Die Stadt sah 1950 ganz anders aus. Bomben hatten fast alle alten Häuser zerstört.* — The city looked completely different in 1950. Bombs had destroyed almost all the old houses.

Do not use it just because something is "long ago". A whole story set in 1945 is told in the simple past. You only switch to the past perfect when you step back from your story's time to something earlier. This is the **[[sequence of tenses]]** in a narrative:

| timeline | tense | example |
|---|---|---|
| now | present | *Heute ist Berlin wieder eine Stadt.* |
| the story's time | simple past (writing) / perfect (speech) | *1989 fiel die Mauer.* |
| before the story's time | past perfect | *Sie hatte die Stadt 28 Jahre lang geteilt.* |

In speech, Germans are relaxed about this; you will hear the perfect where a book would use the past perfect. In writing, and especially with *nachdem*, keep the rule.

## nachdem: after (+ past perfect)

*nachdem* is a **[[subordinating conjunction]]** like *weil* and *dass*: the verb goes to the end. Its clause describes the earlier action, so its tense is one step further back than the main clause:

| *nachdem* clause | main clause |
|---|---|
| past perfect | simple past or perfect |
| perfect | present (or future) |

- *Nachdem die Mauer gefallen war, reisten viele Ostdeutsche zum ersten Mal in den Westen.* — After the Wall had fallen, many East Germans travelled to the West for the first time.
- *Nachdem er das Abitur gemacht hatte, begann er eine Ausbildung.* — After he had done his school-leaving exam, he started an apprenticeship.
- *Nachdem ich gegessen habe, mache ich einen Spaziergang.* — After I've eaten, I go for a walk. (a habit in the present)

When the *nachdem* clause comes first, it fills position 1, so the main verb follows immediately: *Nachdem …, reisten viele …* (verb, comma, verb).

Two warnings:

- *nachdem* is a conjunction (it introduces a clause with a verb). *nach* is a preposition (it is followed by a noun): *nach dem Krieg* (after the war) but *nachdem der Krieg zu Ende war*.
- *danach* and *anschließend* are adverbs meaning "after that, afterwards". They do not join two clauses; they stand in a main clause and push the verb into position 2: *Er machte das Abitur. Danach begann er eine Ausbildung.*

## bevor: before

*bevor* is the opposite: its clause describes the *later* action. Because "later" needs no special tense, *bevor* simply takes the same tense as the main clause.

- *Bevor die Mauer gebaut wurde, konnte man frei von Ost- nach Westberlin gehen.* — Before the Wall was built, you could walk freely from East to West Berlin.
- *Mein Großvater floh, bevor der Krieg zu Ende war.* — My grandfather fled before the war was over.
- *Bevor du gehst, mach bitte das Licht aus.* — Before you go, please turn off the light.

Again: *bevor* is the conjunction; *vor* is the preposition (*vor dem Krieg*, before the war); *vorher* and *zuvor* are adverbs (beforehand, previously).

## Time adverbs: vorher, zuvor, anschließend

These adverbs place an action on the timeline without a second clause. They go in position 1 or in the middle of the sentence.

| adverb | meaning | example |
|---|---|---|
| *vorher* | before, beforehand | *Wir besuchten das Museum. Vorher hatten wir einen Film über die Mauer gesehen.* |
| *zuvor* | before, previously (more formal) | *Zwei Jahre zuvor hatte sie ihr Studium beendet.* |
| *anschließend* | afterwards, then | *Erst gab es eine Rede, anschließend spielte eine Band.* |
| *danach* | after that | *Danach wurde es still.* |
| *damals* | back then, at that time | *Damals gab es zwei deutsche Staaten.* |

*zuvor* often follows a time expression: *ein Jahr zuvor* (a year earlier), *kurz zuvor* (shortly before), *wie nie zuvor* (as never before). The adjective *damalig* (of that time) goes before a noun: *die damalige Regierung* — the government of the time.

## Talking about history

Some words you need to describe the past of a country. Notice how often the past perfect appears when a history text explains the background:

- *Das 20. Jahrhundert war eine Epoche der Kriege und Revolutionen.* — The 20th century was an era of wars and revolutions.
- *Nach dem Zweiten Weltkrieg bauten die Menschen die zerstörten Städte wieder auf.* — After the Second World War people rebuilt the destroyed cities.
- *Viele Soldaten und noch mehr Zivilisten hatten den Krieg nicht überlebt.* — Many soldiers and even more civilians had not survived the war.
- *Die Teilung Deutschlands dauerte vier Jahrzehnte.* — The division of Germany lasted four decades.
- *Zeitzeugen berichten, wie die Diktatur ihren Alltag kontrolliert hatte.* — Contemporary witnesses report how the dictatorship had controlled their everyday life.
- *Nach der Flucht lebten viele Flüchtlinge jahrelang in Lagern.* — After the escape many refugees lived in camps for years.
- *Am 3. Oktober feiert Deutschland den Tag der Deutschen Einheit, den Jahrestag der Wiedervereinigung.* — On 3 October Germany celebrates the Day of German Unity, the anniversary of reunification.
- *Jede Generation erinnert sich anders an diese Zeit.* — Every generation remembers this time differently.

*aufbauen* is separable (*sie bauten auf*); *zerstören* and *überleben* are inseparable, so their participles have no *ge-*: *zerstört, überlebt*. *fliehen* is strong and takes *sein*: *floh, ist geflohen*. *die Folge* means "consequence" and also "episode" of a TV series; *zur Folge haben* = to result in.

## Text: Ein Zeitzeuge erzählt

A school class interviewed a man who grew up in East Berlin. Here is part of the article they wrote for the school website.

> Herr Brandt wurde 1958 in Ostberlin geboren. Drei Jahre später baute die Regierung der DDR die Mauer. Seine Tante war kurz zuvor mit ihren Kindern in den Westen geflohen, und die Familie sah sie fast drei Jahrzehnte lang nicht mehr. „Für mich war die Mauer einfach normal“, erzählte er uns. „Ich kannte die Zeit davor ja nicht.“
>
> Nachdem er die Schule beendet hatte, wurde er Elektriker. Er hatte eine Wohnung, eine Arbeit und Freunde, aber keine Freiheit. Reisen in den Westen waren verboten, und wer die Regierung kritisierte, bekam Probleme. 1989 änderte sich alles. Im Sommer waren schon Tausende über Ungarn geflohen, im Herbst gingen in Leipzig und Berlin immer mehr Menschen auf die Straße. Am Abend des 9. November hörte Herr Brandt im Radio, dass die Grenze offen war. „Zuerst dachte ich, das ist ein Witz“, sagte er. Anschließend lief er mit seinen Nachbarn zum Grenzübergang. Um Mitternacht stand er zum ersten Mal in Westberlin, und seine Tante, die er seit 28 Jahren nicht gesehen hatte, wartete schon auf ihn.
>
> Die Wende hatte für ihn aber auch Folgen, die er vorher nicht erwartet hatte: 1991 verlor er seine Stelle. „Die Freiheit war das Wichtigste“, sagt er heute. „Aber leicht war die Zeit danach nicht.“

Translation:

> Mr Brandt was born in East Berlin in 1958. Three years later the GDR government built the Wall. His aunt had fled to the West with her children shortly before, and the family didn't see her again for almost three decades. "For me the Wall was just normal," he told us. "After all, I didn't know the time before it."
>
> After he had finished school, he became an electrician. He had a flat, a job and friends, but no freedom. Travel to the West was forbidden, and anyone who criticised the government got into trouble. In 1989 everything changed. In the summer thousands had already fled via Hungary, and in the autumn more and more people took to the streets in Leipzig and Berlin. On the evening of 9 November Mr Brandt heard on the radio that the border was open. "At first I thought it was a joke," he said. Then he ran with his neighbours to the border crossing. At midnight he stood in West Berlin for the first time, and his aunt, whom he had not seen for 28 years, was already waiting for him.
>
> But for him the Wende also had consequences that he had not expected beforehand: in 1991 he lost his job. "Freedom was the most important thing," he says today. "But the time afterwards wasn't easy."

Notes: the main story is in the simple past (*baute, sah, wurde, änderte sich, hörte, lief, stand, verlor*). Each past perfect steps back to something earlier: the aunt *had* fled before the Wall, he *had* finished school before becoming an electrician, thousands *had* fled before the autumn protests. The class quotes him in the present tense where he speaks today. *die DDR* (Deutsche Demokratische Republik) = the GDR, East Germany; *der Grenzübergang* = border crossing; *der Witz* = joke; *auf die Straße gehen* = to protest, to take to the streets; *die Wende* = the turning point, the name Germans give to the changes of 1989–90 that led to reunification in 1990.

## Pronunciation

- *das Jahrhundert*: JAHR-hun-dert; *das Jahrzehnt*: jahr-ZEHNT, stress on the second part.
- *die Epoche*: e-PO-che, with *ch* as in *ach*.
- *die Revolution*: re-vo-lu-TSION; *-tion* is always [tsjoːn].
- *fliehen, floh, geflohen*: the *h* is silent; *floh* has a long *o*.
- *der Flüchtling*: FLÜCHT-ling, a short *ü*.

## Common mistakes

- Using *haben* with a *sein* verb: ~~Er hatte geflohen~~ → *Er war geflohen.* The choice of helper is the same as in the perfect.
- Using the past perfect for everything old: ~~1945 hatte der Krieg geendet~~ in the middle of a story about 1945 → *1945 endete der Krieg.* Use it only to look back from the story's time.
- The same tense in *nachdem* and the main clause: ~~Nachdem er aß, ging er~~ → *Nachdem er gegessen hatte, ging er.*
- Mixing up *nachdem* and *nach*: ~~Nachdem dem Krieg~~ → *Nach dem Krieg* (noun) or *Nachdem der Krieg vorbei war* (clause).
- Verb position after *danach* and *anschließend*: they are adverbs, not conjunctions, so the verb comes straight after them: ~~Danach er ging nach Hause~~ → *Danach ging er nach Hause.*
- Translating "before" with *vor* + clause: ~~Vor ich gehe …~~ → *Bevor ich gehe …*

## Key points

- Past perfect = *hatte* / *war* + participle: *ich hatte gesehen, sie war geflohen*. Same helper as in the perfect.
- It describes an action before another past action; the story itself stays in the simple past.
- *nachdem* + past perfect, main clause in the simple past or perfect. *nachdem* + perfect, main clause in the present.
- *bevor* takes the same tense as the main clause.
- Conjunctions *nachdem, bevor* (verb at the end) vs prepositions *nach, vor* (+ noun) vs adverbs *danach, anschließend, vorher, zuvor* (verb in position 2).

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: While, since, until: time clauses
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

You can already join two events in time with *als* and *wenn* (A2) and with *nachdem* and *bevor* (last lesson). This lesson completes the set with *während* (while), *seit* / *seitdem* (since), *bis* (until), *sobald* (as soon as) and *solange* (as long as). With these you can say exactly how two events relate in time: one during the other, one starting from the other, one ending when the other begins.

All of them introduce a **[[temporal clause]]**: a subordinate clause that answers *Wann? Seit wann? Bis wann? Wie lange?* The good news is that the word order is the one you know from *weil* and *dass*. The theme is family life across the generations: grandparents, in-laws, raising children and caring for older relatives.

## Word order: the same for all of them

Every time conjunction in this lesson is a **[[subordinating conjunction]]**. Its clause ends with the conjugated verb, and if the clause comes first, the main clause starts with its verb.

| | main clause | subordinate clause |
|---|---|---|
| clause second | *Ich koche,* | *während die Kinder schlafen.* |
| clause first | *Während die Kinder schlafen,* | *koche ich.* |

With a separable verb, the verb joins its prefix at the end (*sobald er ankommt*); with a modal or a perfect, the conjugated verb is last of all (*bis sie laufen konnte*, *seit sie umgezogen ist*). A comma always separates the two clauses.

## während: while

*während* links two things happening at the same time.

- *Während meine Eltern arbeiteten, passte meine Oma auf uns auf.* — While my parents were at work, my grandma looked after us.
- *Mein Vater liest Zeitung, während er frühstückt.* — My father reads the paper while he has breakfast.

*während* can also contrast two people or things, like English "whereas": *Während meine Schwester sehr ordentlich ist, lebe ich lieber im Chaos.* — Whereas my sister is very tidy, I prefer to live in chaos.

You will meet *während* again in module 3 as a preposition (*während des Urlaubs*, during the holiday). As a conjunction it is followed by a subject and a verb; as a preposition, by a noun.

## seit / seitdem: since

*seit* and *seitdem* mean exactly the same as conjunctions; use whichever you like. Watch the tense: if the situation is still going on, German uses the present, where English uses "have been" or "has been".

- *Seit meine Großeltern in Rente sind, reisen sie viel.* — Since my grandparents retired, they have been travelling a lot.
- *Seitdem wir ein Baby haben, schlafen wir kaum.* — Since we've had a baby, we've hardly been sleeping.
- *Seit sie ins Pflegeheim gezogen ist, besuche ich sie jeden Sonntag.* — Since she moved into the care home, I've visited her every Sunday.

In the last example the move is a single finished event (perfect), but the visiting continues (present). This is the same logic you know from the preposition *seit*: *Ich wohne seit 2020 hier* (I've lived here since 2020).

*seitdem* also works as an adverb in a main clause, meaning "since then", with the verb straight after it: *Er hat 2019 geheiratet. Seitdem lebt er in Graz.* — He got married in 2019. Since then he's lived in Graz.

## bis: until

*bis* marks the point when something stops.

- *Wir haben bei meinen Schwiegereltern gewohnt, bis wir eine eigene Wohnung gefunden haben.* — We lived with my in-laws until we found a flat of our own.
- *Warte, bis ich zurück bin!* — Wait until I'm back!
- *Es dauert noch zehn Minuten, bis das Essen fertig ist.* — It'll be ten minutes until the food is ready.

English often says "not … until" for "only when": *She didn't start talking until she was three.* German uses *erst, als* or *erst, wenn* for this, not *bis*: *Sie hat erst gesprochen, als sie drei war.* Don't translate "not until" word for word.

## sobald: as soon as

*sobald* says that the second event follows immediately.

- *Sobald der Kleine schläft, rufe ich dich an.* — As soon as the little one's asleep, I'll call you.
- *Sobald ich die Nachricht bekommen hatte, fuhr ich ins Krankenhaus.* — As soon as I had got the message, I drove to the hospital.

When the main clause is about the future, the *sobald* clause is often in the perfect, to show it will be finished first: *Sobald ich die Prüfung bestanden habe, mache ich Urlaub.* — As soon as I've passed the exam, I'll go on holiday.

## solange: as long as

*solange* says that two things last for the same period. It often has a sense of condition: "as long as this is true, that is true".

- *Solange du in meinem Haus wohnst, hilfst du im Haushalt.* — As long as you live in my house, you help with the housework.
- *Meine Mutter will zu Hause bleiben, solange sie sich selbst versorgen kann.* — My mother wants to stay at home as long as she can look after herself.

Don't confuse *solange* (one word, conjunction) with *so lange* (two words, "so long, for such a long time"): *Ich habe so lange gewartet!* — I waited for such a long time!

## als and wenn: a quick review

These two are the most common time conjunctions, and they still cause mistakes at B1.

| | one time | more than once |
|---|---|---|
| past | *als*: *Als ich zehn war, bekam ich einen Hund.* | *wenn*: *Wenn wir Oma besuchten, gab es immer Kuchen.* |
| present / future | *wenn*: *Wenn du ankommst, ruf mich an.* | *wenn*: *Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.* |

Only one box takes *als*: a single event (or period) in the past. Everything else is *wenn*. A tip: if you can add *jedes Mal* (every time), it's *wenn*.

## Overview

| conjunction | meaning | typical tense pattern |
|---|---|---|
| *als* | when (once, past) | simple past + simple past |
| *wenn* | when, whenever, if | any |
| *während* | while; whereas | same tense in both |
| *seit, seitdem* | since | present if it continues |
| *bis* | until | same tense in both |
| *sobald* | as soon as | earlier action: perfect / past perfect |
| *solange* | as long as | same tense in both |
| *bevor* | before | same tense in both |
| *nachdem* | after | one step further back |

## Family words

The family vocabulary of A1 covered parents, children and siblings. At B1 you need the wider family and the words for how families live together.

- *Meine Großeltern haben fünf Enkelkinder: drei Enkel und zwei Enkelinnen.* — My grandparents have five grandchildren: three grandsons and two granddaughters.
- *Mein Onkel und meine Tante haben zwei Kinder, also habe ich einen Cousin und eine Cousine.* — My uncle and aunt have two children, so I have a male cousin and a female cousin.
- *Meine Schwester hat einen Sohn und eine Tochter. Ich bin also Tante von einem Neffen und einer Nichte.* — My sister has a son and a daughter. So I'm the aunt of a nephew and a niece.
- *Seit der Hochzeit verstehe ich mich gut mit meiner Schwiegermutter, mit meinem Schwiegervater leider nicht.* — Since the wedding I've got on well with my mother-in-law, but unfortunately not with my father-in-law.
- *Sind Sie mit Herrn Weber verwandt?* — *Ja, er ist ein entfernter Verwandter.* — Are you related to Mr Weber? Yes, he's a distant relative.

- *Nach 40 Jahren Ehe kennen sich die beiden sehr gut.* — After 40 years of marriage the two of them know each other very well. (*der Ehemann* = husband, *die Ehefrau* = wife; in everyday speech *mein Mann, meine Frau*.)
- *Als alleinerziehende Mutter braucht sie Hilfe: Ihre Eltern betreuen das Kind zweimal pro Woche.* — As a single mother she needs help: her parents look after the child twice a week.
- *Er pflegt seinen kranken Vater, seit er in Rente ist.* — He has been caring for his sick father since he retired.
- *Für die Erziehung der Kinder sind heute beide Eltern verantwortlich; früher war das oft die Rolle der Mutter.* — Today both parents are responsible for bringing up the children; in the past that was often the mother's role.
- *Mein Großvater war immer mein Vorbild.* — My grandfather was always my role model.

*der Verwandte* is an **[[adjectival noun]]** like *der Bekannte* (A2): *der Verwandte, ein Verwandter, die Verwandten*. Lesson 5 explains these in detail. *der Cousin* is pronounced as in French [kuˈzɛ̃ː], *die Cousine* [kuˈziːnə].

## Text: Drei Generationen unter einem Dach

A reader wrote to a magazine column about family life.

> Seit meine Mutter vor zwei Jahren gestürzt ist, wohnt sie bei uns. Mein Mann und ich haben lange überlegt, bevor wir uns entschieden haben, denn wir haben zwei Kinder im Teenageralter und arbeiten beide Vollzeit. Am Anfang war es schwierig. Meine Mutter hatte ihr ganzes Leben allein gewohnt und musste sich erst an den Lärm gewöhnen. Und wir mussten uns daran gewöhnen, dass jemand anderes mitredet, wenn es um die Erziehung der Kinder geht.
>
> Inzwischen haben wir eine gute Routine. Während ich im Büro bin, kocht meine Mutter manchmal für alle, solange es ihr gut geht. Die Pflege übernimmt morgens ein Pflegedienst, abends helfe ich ihr. Sobald die Kinder aus der Schule kommen, erzählt sie ihnen Geschichten von früher, und mein Sohn, der sich sonst für nichts interessiert, hört zu. Das Verhältnis zwischen Oma und Enkeln ist so eng wie nie zuvor.
>
> Natürlich gibt es auch Konflikte. Meine Mutter hat ihre Gewohnheiten, und mein Mann hat manchmal das Gefühl, dass seine Schwiegermutter die Rolle der Chefin spielt. Aber bis wir eine bessere Lösung finden, bleibt es so. Und ehrlich gesagt: Ich glaube, wir alle haben viel gelernt.

Translation:

> Since my mother fell two years ago, she has been living with us. My husband and I thought about it for a long time before we decided, because we have two teenage children and both work full time. At first it was difficult. My mother had lived alone all her life and first had to get used to the noise. And we had to get used to someone else having a say when it comes to bringing up the children.
>
> Now we have a good routine. While I'm at the office, my mother sometimes cooks for everyone, as long as she's feeling well. A care service takes care of the nursing in the morning; in the evening I help her. As soon as the children come home from school, she tells them stories from the old days, and my son, who usually isn't interested in anything, listens. The relationship between grandma and grandchildren is closer than ever.
>
> Of course there are conflicts too. My mother has her habits, and my husband sometimes feels that his mother-in-law plays the role of the boss. But until we find a better solution, it'll stay like this. And to be honest: I think we've all learned a lot.

Notes: *stürzen* (ist gestürzt) = to fall (and hurt yourself); *überlegen* = to think about, consider; *mitreden* = to have a say; *inzwischen* = by now, meanwhile; *der Pflegedienst* = home-care service; *eng* = close, tight; *wie nie zuvor* = than ever before. *sich gewöhnen an* + accusative = to get used to; with a clause, use *daran*: *sich daran gewöhnen, dass …*

## Pronunciation

- *sobald*: so-BALD, stress on the second syllable; *solange*: so-LAN-ge.
- *während*: a long *ä*, WÄH-rend. The *h* only shows the vowel is long.
- *die Erziehung*: er-ZIE-hung; *der Haushalt*: HAUS-halt.
- *die Nichte*: *ch* as in *ich*; *der Neffe*: short *e*, NEF-fe.

## Common mistakes

- Verb in second position after the conjunction: ~~während ich bin im Büro~~ → *während ich im Büro bin*.
- Past tense with *seit* for something still true: ~~Seit ich hier wohnte, …~~ → *Seit ich hier wohne, …*
- *bis* for "not until": ~~Sie hat nicht gesprochen, bis sie drei war~~ is understandable but unnatural; say *Sie hat erst mit drei gesprochen* or *erst, als sie drei war*.
- *wenn* for a single past event: ~~Wenn ich zehn war~~ → *Als ich zehn war*.
- Forgetting the verb-first main clause: ~~Sobald er kommt, wir essen~~ → *Sobald er kommt, essen wir.*
- Writing *solange* as two words when you mean "as long as": *solange du hier wohnst*.

## Key points

- *während* (while, whereas), *seit/seitdem* (since), *bis* (until), *sobald* (as soon as), *solange* (as long as) all send the verb to the end.
- Subordinate clause first → main clause starts with the verb: *Sobald er kommt, essen wir.*
- *seit/seitdem* + present for a situation that still continues.
- *seitdem* can also be an adverb in a main clause: "since then".
- *als* = one time in the past; *wenn* = every other case.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: The future: werden + infinitive
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

So far this module has looked back: stories, history, family memories. Now we look ahead. At A2 you met *werden* + infinitive briefly for plans; at B1 you need it properly, because it does more than talk about the future. Germans use it to make predictions, to promise, to announce firm intentions and, very often, to guess what is probably true *right now*.

You will also see why German speakers use the **[[future tense]]** less than English speakers, and how to tell apart the three jobs of *werden*: a full verb (to become), the future, and, as a preview, the passive. The theme is technology and science: inventions, robots, artificial intelligence, research and forecasts.

## The form

The future (*Futur I*) is a form of *werden* in position 2 and the infinitive at the end of the clause.

| | werden | | infinitive |
|---|---|---|---|
| ich | werde | … | arbeiten |
| du | wirst | … | arbeiten |
| er / sie / es | wird | … | arbeiten |
| wir | werden | … | arbeiten |
| ihr | werdet | … | arbeiten |
| sie / Sie | werden | … | arbeiten |

Watch the irregular forms: *du wirst* (no *d*) and *er wird* (no extra *-et*).

- *Roboter werden viele Arbeiten im Haushalt übernehmen.* — Robots will take over many household tasks.
- *Ich werde dich morgen anrufen.* — I'll call you tomorrow.

The verb bracket works as usual. A separable verb stays together at the end (*Er wird morgen ankommen*). With a modal verb, the modal infinitive is last: *Wir werden mehr Energie sparen müssen.* — We'll have to save more energy. In a subordinate clause *werden* goes to the very end: *Ich glaube, dass die Technik unser Leben weiter verändern wird.*

## When Germans use it, and when they don't

English uses "will" or "going to" almost every time it talks about the future. German doesn't. For plans and arrangements, especially with a time word, the present tense is normal:

- *Morgen fahre ich nach Hamburg.* — Tomorrow I'm going to Hamburg.
- *Nächstes Jahr studiere ich in Wien.* — Next year I'm studying in Vienna.
- *Das Meeting beginnt um zehn.* — The meeting starts at ten.

*Morgen werde ich nach Hamburg fahren* is not wrong, but it sounds heavier, as if you were making an announcement. The future with *werden* is the right choice in these cases:

| use | example | English |
|---|---|---|
| prediction (no time word needed) | *Es wird bald regnen.* | It's going to rain soon. |
| forecast in news and science | *Die Bevölkerung wird bis 2050 wachsen.* | The population will grow until 2050. |
| promise | *Ich werde dir helfen, versprochen.* | I'll help you, I promise. |
| firm intention, resolution | *Ab Montag werde ich weniger Zeit am Handy verbringen.* | From Monday I'm going to spend less time on my phone. |
| strong instruction (to a child, a team) | *Du wirst jetzt sofort dein Zimmer aufräumen!* | You're going to tidy your room right now! |

Rule of thumb: if a time word already makes the future clear and it's a plan, use the present. If you predict, promise or announce, use *werden*.

## Guessing about now: werden + wohl

German also uses the future form to make an assumption about the present. You are not sure, but you think something is probably true. The little word *wohl* (probably, I suppose) or *sicher* (surely) usually comes with it.

- *Wo ist Jan?* — *Er wird wohl noch im Labor sein.* — Where's Jan? He's probably still in the lab.
- *Das Paket ist nicht da. Es wird wohl morgen kommen.* — The parcel isn't here. It'll probably come tomorrow.
- *Sie antwortet nicht. Sie wird schon schlafen.* — She's not answering. She'll be asleep already.
- *Das wird schon stimmen.* — That's probably right. / I'm sure that's right.

English does something very similar: "That'll be the postman" means "That's probably the postman". When you hear *wird wohl* + a present situation, think "probably".

Other words that soften a statement: *wahrscheinlich* (probably), *vermutlich* (presumably), *voraussichtlich* (expected, according to plan; used in timetables and news), *bestimmt* (certainly). They work with the present or the future:

- *Der Zug hat voraussichtlich 20 Minuten Verspätung.* — The train is expected to be 20 minutes late.
- *Vermutlich hat er die E-Mail nicht gelesen.* — Presumably he hasn't read the e-mail.
- *Die Forscher werden wahrscheinlich nächstes Jahr Ergebnisse veröffentlichen.* — The researchers will probably publish results next year.

## The three jobs of werden

*werden* is one of the busiest verbs in German. Ask what comes with it:

| werden + … | job | example | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| noun or adjective | full verb: *to become* | *Sie wird Ingenieurin. Es wird kalt.* | She's becoming an engineer. It's getting cold. |
| infinitive | future | *Sie wird das Problem lösen.* | She will solve the problem. |
| past participle | passive *(preview)* | *Das Auto wird in Bayern gebaut.* | The car is built in Bavaria. |

You met the full verb at A2 (*Ich will Ärztin werden*). The passive comes in module 4; for now, just notice the participle (*gebaut*) and don't read it as "will". The future of the full verb uses *werden* twice, and that is fine: *Es wird kalt werden.* — It's going to get cold.

## Technology and science words

- *Die Wissenschaftlerin forscht seit Jahren an künstlicher Intelligenz.* — The scientist has been researching artificial intelligence for years. (*forschen an* + dative)
- *Wer hat das Telefon erfunden?* — *Viele sagen: Alexander Graham Bell. Aber die Erfindung hat eine lange Geschichte.* — Who invented the telephone? Many say Alexander Graham Bell. But the invention has a long history.
- *Die Firma entwickelt eine neue Technologie für Elektroautos.* — The company is developing a new technology for electric cars.
- *Die Digitalisierung hat den Alltag stark verändert.* — Digitalisation has changed everyday life a lot.
- *Werden Roboter eines Tages Lehrer ersetzen?* — Will robots replace teachers one day?
- *Die Raumfahrt hat in den letzten Jahrzehnten große Fortschritte gemacht.* — Spaceflight has made great progress in recent decades.
- *Eine Rakete bringt die Astronauten ins Weltall. Von dort sieht die Erde ganz klein aus.* — A rocket takes the astronauts into space. From there the Earth looks very small.
- *Ist es auf einem anderen Planeten möglich zu leben?* — Is it possible to live on another planet?
- *Im Labor machen die Studenten ein Experiment. Ein Programm wertet die Daten automatisch aus.* — In the lab the students do an experiment. A program analyses the data automatically.

*die Technik* is technology in general and also engineering and technique (*die Technik eines Sportlers*); *die Technologie* is usually a particular technology (*Solartechnologie*). *erfinden* is strong: *erfand, hat erfunden*. *ersetzen* is weak and inseparable: *ersetzte, hat ersetzt*. *vorhersagen* is separable: *Er sagt das Wetter vorher*, *hat vorhergesagt*.

## Text: Unser Alltag im Jahr 2050

A science blog asked a researcher about the future.

> Wie werden wir in 25 Jahren leben? Prognosen sind schwierig, sagt die Informatikerin Dr. Lea Hartmann, denn die Entwicklung der Technik geht schneller, als die meisten Experten vorhersagen. Trotzdem wagt sie ein paar Aussagen.
>
> „Künstliche Intelligenz wird ein ganz normaler Teil unseres Alltags sein, so wie heute das Smartphone. Viele einfache Bürojobs werden verschwinden, aber es werden auch neue Berufe entstehen, die wir uns heute noch gar nicht vorstellen können.“ Roboter werden ältere Menschen im Haushalt unterstützen, glaubt sie. „Ersetzen werden sie die Pflegekräfte aber nicht. Menschen brauchen Menschen.“
>
> Auch in der Medizin erwartet sie große Fortschritte. Ärzte werden Krankheiten mithilfe von Daten früher erkennen, und neue Medikamente werden schneller entwickelt. Und die Raumfahrt? „Ein Besuch auf dem Mond wird für reiche Touristen wohl möglich sein. Auf dem Mars werden wir 2050 vermutlich noch nicht wohnen.“
>
> Eine Sache ist für Dr. Hartmann sicher: „Die Technologie allein wird die Welt nicht besser machen. Wir werden entscheiden müssen, wie wir sie nutzen.“ Und ihr eigenes Leben? Sie lacht. „Ich werde im Jahr 2050 hoffentlich im Garten sitzen. Ohne Computer.“

Translation:

> How will we live in 25 years? Forecasts are difficult, says the computer scientist Dr Lea Hartmann, because the development of technology moves faster than most experts predict. All the same, she risks a few statements.
>
> "Artificial intelligence will be a completely normal part of our everyday life, just like the smartphone today. Many simple office jobs will disappear, but new professions will also emerge that we can't even imagine today." Robots will support older people in the household, she believes. "But they won't replace care workers. People need people."
>
> She also expects great progress in medicine. Doctors will recognise illnesses earlier with the help of data, and new medicines will be developed faster. And spaceflight? "A visit to the moon will probably be possible for rich tourists. We probably won't be living on Mars by 2050."
>
> One thing is certain for Dr Hartmann: "Technology alone won't make the world better. We'll have to decide how we use it." And her own life? She laughs. "In 2050 I hope I'll be sitting in the garden. Without a computer."

Notes: *werden … sein, werden verschwinden, werden entstehen, werden unterstützen* are predictions. *werden … entwickelt* (with a participle) is the passive, "will be developed" or "are being developed"; just recognise it. *werden … müssen*: future with a modal. *wagen* = to dare, risk; *die Aussage* = statement; *entstehen* = to come into being, emerge; *sich etwas vorstellen* = to imagine something; *mithilfe von* = with the help of; *nutzen* = to use.

## Pronunciation

- *wirst, wird*: short *i*, and the *d* in *wird* sounds like *t*.
- *die Technik*: TECH-nik, *ch* as in *ich*; *die Technologie*: tech-no-lo-GIE.
- *der Roboter*: RO-bo-ter, stress on the first syllable (not ro-BO-ter).
- *die Prognose*: pro-GNO-se; *das Labor*: la-BOR, stress on the second syllable.
- *der Planet*: pla-NET, stress on the second syllable.

## Common mistakes

- Using *werden* for every future plan: *Morgen werde ich ins Kino gehen* is possible but stiff; *Morgen gehe ich ins Kino* is what people say.
- Confusing *werden* and *wollen*: *Ich will das machen* means "I want to do that", not "I will do that". "I will" is *Ich werde*.
- Wrong forms: ~~du werdest, er werdet~~ → *du wirst, er wird*.
- Infinitive in the middle: ~~Ich werde lernen mehr Deutsch~~ → *Ich werde mehr Deutsch lernen.*
- Reading *wird* + participle as the future: *Das Haus wird gebaut* is "the house is being built", not "will build".
- *wird wohl* as certain: it is a guess. *Er wird wohl krank sein* = he's probably ill.

## Key points

- Future = *werden* (position 2) + infinitive (end): *Es wird regnen.*
- For plans with a time word, Germans usually use the present: *Morgen fahre ich nach Berlin.*
- Use *werden* for predictions, forecasts, promises and firm intentions.
- *werden* + *wohl* (+ present situation) = an assumption: *Er wird wohl im Büro sein.*
- *werden* + noun/adjective = to become; + infinitive = future; + participle = passive.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Weak nouns and adjectival nouns
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Most German nouns change very little when their case changes: *der Tisch, den Tisch, dem Tisch*. Only the article does the work. But there are two groups of nouns for people that behave differently, and you have already met members of both: *Ich frage meinen Kollegen* (not *Kollege*) and *Das ist ein Bekannter von mir* (not *Bekannte*).

The first group are the **[[weak nouns]]**, which add *-n* or *-en* in every case except the nominative singular. The second are **[[adjectival nouns]]**, adjectives used as nouns, which take adjective endings. This lesson explains both, along with the names of nationalities, which use both systems. The theme is people in society: adults and young people, citizens and foreigners, majorities and minorities.

## Weak nouns: the n-declension

A weak noun (the pattern is called the **[[n-declension]]**) is masculine (the one neuter exception, *das Herz*, comes below). It adds *-n* or *-en* everywhere except in the nominative singular.

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| nominative | der Kollege | die Kollegen |
| accusative | den Kollegen | die Kollegen |
| dative | dem Kollegen | den Kollegen |
| genitive | des Kollegen | der Kollegen |

| | singular | plural |
|---|---|---|
| nominative | der Mensch | die Menschen |
| accusative | den Menschen | die Menschen |
| dative | dem Menschen | den Menschen |
| genitive | des Menschen | der Menschen |

- *Ich kenne den Jungen von der Schule.* — I know the boy from school.
- *Die Polizei hat mit dem Zeugen gesprochen.* — The police spoke to the witness.
- *Wir brauchen einen Experten.* — We need an expert.
- *Das Büro des Präsidenten ist im ersten Stock.* — The president's office is on the first floor.

The ending helps the listener: in *Der Hund beißt den Jungen*, the *-n* shows that the boy is the object, even if the word order changes (*Den Jungen beißt der Hund*).

### How to recognise weak nouns

You can't tell from every noun, but three groups cover almost all of them:

| group | examples |
|---|---|
| 1. masculine nouns ending in *-e* for people and animals | *der Junge, der Kollege, der Kunde, der Zeuge, der Experte, der Neffe, der Franzose, der Löwe* |
| 2. masculine foreign words, mostly for people, ending in *-ant, -ent, -ist, -at, -oge, -et* | *der Praktikant, der Student, der Präsident, der Polizist, der Tourist, der Soldat, der Kandidat, der Biologe, der Planet* |
| 3. a few short masculine nouns, to learn one by one | *der Mensch, der Herr, der Nachbar, der Bauer, der Held, der Bär, der Prinz* |

*der Herr* adds only *-n* in the singular but *-en* in the plural: *Ich gebe Herrn Schulz den Brief* (dative singular), *Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren* (plural). *der Nachbar* and *der Bauer* add *-n*: *den Nachbarn, dem Bauern* (female: *die Bäuerin*, farmer).

Watch out: not every masculine noun in *-e* is weak, but the exceptions are rare at B1 (*der Käse* is normal). And feminine nouns are never weak: *die Kollegin, die Kollegin, der Kollegin*.

### The Name group: -ns in the genitive

A handful of weak nouns that are not people add *-ns* in the genitive and otherwise behave like weak nouns: *der Name – den Namen – dem Namen – des Namens*. The others you'll meet are *der Gedanke* (thought), *der Glaube* (belief), *der Buchstabe* (letter of the alphabet) and *der Friede* (peace, usually *der Frieden*). *das Herz* is neuter but similar: *dem Herzen, des Herzens*.

- *Wie war noch mal der Name des Autors?* — What was the author's name again?
- *Ich kann mich an seinen Namen nicht erinnern.* — I can't remember his name.

In everyday speech, people sometimes drop the *-n* (*Ich habe den Präsident gesehen*). In writing and in the exam, use it.

## Adjectival nouns

Any adjective or participle can become a noun: give it a capital letter and an article. It still behaves like an adjective, so its ending changes with the article and case, exactly as you learned in A2.

| | masculine | feminine | plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| with *der/die* | der Erwachsene | die Erwachsene | die Erwachsenen |
| with *ein/eine* | ein Erwachsener | eine Erwachsene | – Erwachsene |
| accusative | den Erwachsenen / einen Erwachsenen | die / eine Erwachsene | die Erwachsenen / Erwachsene |
| dative | dem Erwachsenen / einem Erwachsenen | der / einer Erwachsenen | den Erwachsenen / Erwachsenen |

The two forms that differ from weak nouns are the most important ones: after *ein* the masculine is *-er* (*ein Erwachsener*), and without any article the plural ends in *-e* (*viele Erwachsene, zwei Angestellte*).

- *Der Film ist nichts für Kinder, nur für Erwachsene.* — The film isn't for children, only for adults.
- *Mein Bruder ist Beamter.* — My brother is a civil servant. (no article, like *ein Beamter*)
- *Die Firma hat 200 Angestellte.* — The company has 200 employees.
- *Viele Jugendliche wohnen noch bei ihren Eltern.* — Many young people still live with their parents.
- *Für einen Fremden ist es nicht leicht, Kontakt zu den Einheimischen zu finden.* — For a stranger it isn't easy to make contact with the locals.

Common adjectival nouns for people:

| adjective / participle | person | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *erwachsen* | der / die Erwachsene | adult |
| *jugendlich* | der / die Jugendliche | young person, teenager |
| *angestellt* | der / die Angestellte | employee |
| *bekannt* | der / die Bekannte | acquaintance |
| *verwandt* | der / die Verwandte | relative |
| *fremd* | der / die Fremde | stranger |
| *arbeitslos* | der / die Arbeitslose | unemployed person |
| *einheimisch* | der / die Einheimische | local |
| – | der Beamte (female: *die Beamtin*) | civil servant |

*der Beamte* is the odd one: for a woman, people use the normal noun *die Beamtin*.

### Things and ideas: das Gute, etwas Neues

Neuter adjectival nouns mean a thing or an idea: *das Gute* (the good thing, what's good), *das Wichtigste* (the most important thing), *das Neue* (what's new). After *etwas, nichts, viel, wenig* they take the ending *-es*, and after *alles* the ending *-e*:

- *Gibt es etwas Neues?* — Is there anything new?
- *Heute ist nichts Besonderes passiert.* — Nothing special happened today.
- *Alles Gute zum Geburtstag!* — All the best for your birthday!
- *Das Gute an der Stadt ist, dass alles nah ist.* — The good thing about the city is that everything is close.

## Nationalities

Words for people of different nationalities use three systems. You don't have to guess: most follow the *-er* rule, and the other two groups are small.

| system | male | female | plural |
|---|---|---|---|
| normal noun in *-er* | *der Italiener, der Österreicher, der Schweizer, der Amerikaner* | *die Italienerin …* | *die Italiener* |
| weak noun in *-e* | *der Franzose, der Pole, der Türke, der Grieche, der Russe* | *die Französin, die Polin, die Türkin …* | *die Franzosen* |
| adjectival noun | *der Deutsche, ein Deutscher* | *die Deutsche, eine Deutsche* | *die Deutschen, viele Deutsche* |

*Deutsche* is the only common adjectival nationality noun. *Er ist Deutscher. Sie ist Deutsche. Wir sind Deutsche.* The adjective is *deutsch* with a small letter: *die deutsche Sprache, ein deutsches Auto*. The language is *Deutsch* with a capital: *Ich lerne Deutsch.*

- *Mein Nachbar ist Franzose. Ich habe dem Franzosen gestern mit dem Umzug geholfen.* — My neighbour is French. I helped the Frenchman move yesterday.
- *Die Deutschen trinken viel Mineralwasser.* — Germans drink a lot of mineral water.

## People in society

- *Die Bevölkerung Deutschlands ist älter geworden: Es gibt mehr Rentner und weniger Jugendliche.* — Germany's population has got older: there are more pensioners and fewer young people.
- *Etwa jeder vierte Mensch in Deutschland hat eine ausländische Herkunft.* — About one in four people in Germany has a foreign background.
- *Die Mehrheit der Bürger ist für das Projekt, aber eine Minderheit protestiert.* — The majority of citizens are for the project, but a minority is protesting.
- *Als Ausländer braucht man für manche Berufe besondere Dokumente.* — As a foreigner you need special documents for some jobs.
- *Die Bewohner des Hauses haben eine Gruppe gegründet.* — The residents of the building have started a group.
- *Sie ist Mitglied in einem Verein, der Menschen in Not hilft.* — She is a member of a club that helps people in need.

*die Leute* (people) is plural only and informal: *Die Leute hier sind nett.* *die Menschen* is more general and more formal: *Alle Menschen sind gleich.* For a single person, use *der Mensch* or *die Person*.

## Text: Neu in der Stadt

A blog post on a city's welcome website.

> Ich heiße Karim, ich bin 34 und komme aus Tunesien. Seit drei Jahren lebe ich in Leipzig. Am Anfang war ich hier ein Fremder: Ich kannte keinen Menschen, und mein Deutsch war schlecht. Auf dem Amt habe ich lange mit einem Beamten gesprochen, und ich habe fast nichts verstanden. Zum Glück hatte ich einen Nachbarn, Herrn Krause, einen Rentner, der mir viel geholfen hat. Ohne den Nachbarn hätte ich die ersten Monate nicht geschafft.
>
> Heute arbeite ich als Angestellter in einer IT-Firma. Meine Kollegen kommen aus sieben Ländern, aber die Mehrheit sind Deutsche. Mit einem Kollegen, einem Franzosen, spiele ich jeden Freitag Fußball. Abends gebe ich in einem Jugendzentrum Kurse für Jugendliche, die programmieren lernen wollen.
>
> Was ist das Schönste an Leipzig? Die Leute sind offen, und es passiert immer etwas Neues. Natürlich gibt es auch Menschen, die Ausländer nicht mögen. Aber ich habe gelernt: Man braucht nicht die ganze Gesellschaft, um sich zu Hause zu fühlen. Man braucht ein paar gute Menschen.

Translation:

> My name is Karim, I'm 34 and I'm from Tunisia. I've been living in Leipzig for three years. At first I was a stranger here: I didn't know a single person, and my German was bad. At the authorities' office I talked to an official for a long time and understood almost nothing. Luckily I had a neighbour, Mr Krause, a pensioner, who helped me a lot. Without that neighbour I wouldn't have managed the first months.
>
> Today I work as an employee in an IT company. My colleagues come from seven countries, but the majority are Germans. I play football every Friday with a colleague, a Frenchman. In the evenings I give courses at a youth centre for young people who want to learn programming.
>
> What's the best thing about Leipzig? People are open, and there's always something new happening. Of course there are also people who don't like foreigners. But I've learned: you don't need the whole of society to feel at home. You need a few good people.

Notes: weak nouns: *keinen Menschen, einen Nachbarn, Herrn Krause, den Nachbarn, einem Kollegen, einem Franzosen*. Adjectival nouns: *ein Fremder, einem Beamten, Angestellter, Deutsche, Jugendliche, das Schönste, etwas Neues*. *hätte … nicht geschafft* = wouldn't have managed (Konjunktiv II of the past, module 5); *das Amt* = public office; *um … zu* = in order to (module 2).

## Pronunciation

- *der Mensch*: one syllable; *den Menschen*: MEN-schen.
- *der Erwachsene*: er-WACH-se-ne, *ch* as in *ach*.
- *der Beamte*: be-AM-te, three syllables; the *e* and *a* are pronounced separately.
- *die Bevölkerung*: be-VÖL-ke-rung; *die Gesellschaft*: ge-SELL-schaft.
- *der Franzose*: fran-TSO-se, *z* = [ts].

## Common mistakes

- Forgetting the *-n*: ~~Ich frage den Kollege~~ → *Ich frage den Kollegen.* ~~mit dem Student~~ → *mit dem Studenten.*
- Adding *-n* to the nominative: ~~Der Kollegen ist krank~~ → *Der Kollege ist krank.*
- Treating feminine nouns as weak: ~~der Kolleginnen~~ (singular) → *der Kollegin*.
- Wrong ending after *ein*: ~~ein Erwachsene, ein Deutsche~~ (for a man) → *ein Erwachsener, ein Deutscher*.
- Article in nationality and job statements: ~~Er ist ein Deutscher~~ is possible but *Er ist Deutscher* is the normal form.
- Small letter for the adjectival noun: ~~die deutschen trinken …~~ → *die Deutschen*; but *deutsch* stays small as an adjective.
- *etwas neu* → *etwas Neues*: capital letter and *-es*.

## Key points

- Weak nouns (masculine only) add *-(e)n* in every form except the nominative singular: *der Kollege, den/dem/des Kollegen*.
- Most are people or animals in *-e*, foreign words in *-ent, -ant, -ist, -at, -oge*, plus *Mensch, Herr, Nachbar, Bauer, Held*.
- *der Name, der Gedanke, der Glaube, der Buchstabe*: genitive *-ns*.
- Adjectival nouns take adjective endings: *der Erwachsene, ein Erwachsener, viele Erwachsene*.
- Neuter adjectival nouns are things: *das Gute, etwas Neues, nichts Besonderes, alles Gute*.
- Nationalities: *-er* nouns (*der Italiener*), weak nouns (*der Franzose*) and *der/die Deutsche*.

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Although: obwohl, trotzdem, zwar … aber
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

Module 1 was about telling stories in time. This module is about the logic between ideas: reasons, goals, conditions, choices and contrasts. You already have the basic tools from A2: *weil* and *denn* give a reason, *deshalb* gives a result, *aber* sets up a contrast, and *trotzdem* says "anyway". At B1 you need to argue a little: in a forum post, a discussion with a partner, an opinion in the exam. For that, one more kind of link is essential, the one that says "this is true, and yet the other thing happens too". English uses *although*, *even so*, *admittedly … but*. German uses *obwohl*, *trotzdem* and *zwar … aber*.

The theme is money and shopping decisions: what we spend, what we save, and why we sometimes buy things we can't really afford.

## Review: reason and result

A reason and its result can be linked from either end. You know both from A2:

- *Ich kaufe wenig Kleidung, weil ich sparen will.* — I buy few clothes because I want to save. (*weil*: verb at the end)
- *Ich will sparen, deshalb kaufe ich wenig Kleidung.* — I want to save, so I buy few clothes. (*deshalb*: verb straight after)

A clause with *weil* is a **[[causal clause]]**: it answers *Warum?* The clause with *deshalb* gives the consequence. Hold on to this picture, because the new words in this lesson work in exactly the same two ways, only with the opposite logic.

## obwohl: although

Sometimes the reason should lead to a result, but it doesn't. *Ich habe wenig Geld* should mean *Ich kaufe kein neues Handy*. If you buy one anyway, the logic is broken, and German marks that with *obwohl*:

- *Ich kaufe ein neues Handy, obwohl ich wenig Geld habe.* — I'm buying a new phone although I don't have much money.

A clause like this is a **[[concessive clause]]**: you "concede" a fact (yes, I have little money) but say it doesn't stop the main event. *obwohl* is a subordinating conjunction like *weil*, so the conjugated verb goes to the end:

| main clause | , | *obwohl* | subject | middle | verb at the end |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Lena fährt jedes Jahr in Urlaub* | , | *obwohl* | *sie* | *nicht viel* | *verdient.* |
| *Wir haben das Sofa gekauft* | , | *obwohl* | *es* | *sehr teuer* | *war.* |
| *Er gibt viel Geld für Kleidung aus* | , | *obwohl* | *er* | *Schulden* | *hat.* |
| *Ich esse den Kuchen* | , | *obwohl* | *ich* | *eigentlich keinen Zucker essen* | *will.* |

As with *weil*, a separable verb joins up (*obwohl sie viel Geld ausgibt*), a modal goes last (*obwohl ich sparen muss*), and in the perfect the auxiliary is last (*obwohl er den Kredit bekommen hat*).

The *obwohl* clause can also come first. Then it fills position 1 of the whole sentence and the main verb follows straight after the comma: verb, comma, verb.

- *Obwohl das Kleid preiswert war, habe ich es nicht gekauft.* — Although the dress was good value, I didn't buy it.
- *Obwohl wir sparsam leben, reicht das Geld oft nicht.* — Although we live frugally, the money often isn't enough.

### weil or obwohl?

A quick test: put "and that's why" between the two facts. If it makes sense, use *weil*; if you need "and yet", use *obwohl*.

- *Ich kaufe Bio-Gemüse, weil es gesünder ist.* — healthier, that's why I buy it.
- *Ich kaufe Bio-Gemüse, obwohl es teurer ist.* — dearer, and yet I buy it.

## trotzdem: the same idea from the other end

*trotzdem* (anyway, nevertheless, even so) is the partner of *obwohl*, just as *deshalb* is the partner of *weil*. It is a linking adverb, so it takes position 1 and the verb comes straight after it. It introduces the surprising result, not the fact:

- *Ich habe wenig Geld. Trotzdem kaufe ich ein neues Handy.* — I don't have much money. I'm buying a new phone anyway.
- *Das Hotel war teuer, trotzdem waren wir nicht zufrieden.* — The hotel was expensive, but even so we weren't happy.

| | reason → expected result | fact → unexpected result |
|---|---|---|
| subordinating (verb last) | *weil* | *obwohl* |
| adverb (verb straight after) | *deshalb* | *trotzdem* |

Watch which half each word belongs to. *obwohl* sits in front of the fact (*obwohl ich wenig Geld habe*); *trotzdem* sits in front of the result (*trotzdem kaufe ich …*). The same pair of facts, two ways:

- *Obwohl der Lohn niedrig ist, arbeitet sie gern dort.*
- *Der Lohn ist niedrig. Trotzdem arbeitet sie gern dort.* — The pay is low. She likes working there all the same.

*trotzdem* can also stand later in the sentence, after the verb: *Sie arbeitet trotzdem gern dort.* In more formal writing you'll find two synonyms, *dennoch* (all the same) and *jedoch* (however): *Die Preise sind gestiegen. Dennoch kaufen viele Menschen mehr als früher.* *jedoch* is more like *aber* and can also stand after the verb: *Das Angebot war gut, die Qualität jedoch nicht.*

### Preview: trotz + noun

There is also a preposition, *trotz* (despite, in spite of), which you'll meet properly in lesson 14. It is followed by a noun, not a clause: *Trotz des Regens sind wir einkaufen gegangen.* — Despite the rain, we went shopping. In everyday speech many people say *trotz dem Regen*. For now, just recognise it: *obwohl* + clause, *trotz* + noun.

## zwar … aber: admittedly …, but

When you want to give one point to the other side before you make your own, use *zwar … aber*. *zwar* goes in the first clause, usually right after the verb; *aber* starts the second:

- *Das Auto ist zwar alt, aber es fährt noch gut.* — The car may be old, but it still runs well.
- *Ich verdiene zwar nicht viel, aber ich komme gut zurecht.* — I admittedly don't earn much, but I get by fine.
- *Der Kredit ist zwar günstig, aber die Laufzeit ist sehr lang.* — It's true the loan is cheap, but it runs for a very long time.

This is a **[[two-part connector]]**, a pair of words that work together (lesson 9 brings more of them). *zwar* has no exact English translation; it tells the listener "I'm conceding this, and a *but* is coming". *zwar* can also stand in position 1 (*Zwar ist das Auto alt, aber …*), but after the verb is much more common. Don't put *zwar* without an *aber* (or *doch, jedoch*) following: the listener waits for it.

*zwar … aber* is perfect for discussions and the exam forum post, because it sounds balanced: *Online-Shopping ist zwar bequem, aber man sieht die Qualität nicht.*

## Money: words and set phrases

| German | English |
|---|---|
| *das Einkommen* / *der Lohn* | income / wage, pay |
| *die Einnahmen* / *die Ausgaben* | income, takings / expenses (usually plural) |
| *die Steuer*, *Steuern zahlen* | tax, to pay taxes |
| *der Kredit*, *einen Kredit aufnehmen* | loan, to take out a loan |
| *die Schulden*, *Schulden machen* | debts, to get into debt |
| *verschuldet sein* | to be in debt |
| *der Zins*, *die Zinsen* | interest |
| *die Ersparnisse* | savings |

Some verbs to know well:

- *Geld für etwas ausgeben* — to spend money on something: *Wie viel gibst du im Monat für Essen aus?* — How much do you spend a month on food? Separable and strong: *er gibt aus, er gab aus, er hat ausgegeben*.
- *sich etwas leisten (können)* — to (be able to) afford something. The reflexive pronoun is dative: *Ich kann mir kein Auto leisten.* — I can't afford a car. *Gönn dir was! Leiste dir mal etwas!* — Treat yourself!
- *auf etwas verzichten* — to do without something: *Ich verzichte auf Fleisch.*
- *Das lohnt sich.* — It's worth it. *Lohnt es sich, ein teures Fahrrad zu kaufen?*
- *verschwenden* — to waste: *Wir verschwenden zu viel Geld für Kaffee to go.*
- *jemanden überzeugen* — to convince: *Die Werbung hat mich nicht überzeugt.*

The word *der Konsum* means consumption (of goods); *der Verbraucher / die Verbraucherin* is the consumer. You'll often see *Verbraucherschutz* (consumer protection) and *nachhaltiger Konsum* (sustainable consumption) in German newspapers.

## A blog post: Ein Jahr ohne Neukauf

> Vor einem Jahr habe ich ein Experiment gestartet: zwölf Monate lang keine neue Kleidung, keine neuen Geräte, kein Luxus. Der Grund war einfach. Obwohl ich ein gutes Einkommen habe, war am Ende des Monats nie Geld übrig. Ich hatte zwar keine Schulden, aber auch keine Ersparnisse.
>
> Also habe ich alle Ausgaben aufgeschrieben. Das Ergebnis hat mich schockiert: Ich habe fast 200 Euro im Monat für Dinge ausgegeben, die ich nicht gebraucht habe. Oft waren es Schnäppchen. Ein Pullover für 9 Euro ist zwar preiswert, aber wenn man ihn nie trägt, ist er trotzdem verschwendetes Geld.
>
> Am Anfang war es schwer. Wenn meine Freundinnen shoppen gegangen sind, bin ich trotzdem mitgegangen, und ich habe nichts gekauft. Inzwischen verzichte ich gern. Wenn etwas kaputtgeht, repariere ich es oder ich kaufe es gebraucht. Ich vergleiche heute viel mehr: Brauche ich das wirklich? Gibt es eine bessere Qualität, die länger hält?
>
> Bin ich jetzt ein besserer Mensch? Nein. Aber ich habe in einem Jahr 2.300 Euro gespart, und das hat sich gelohnt. Ich kann mir jetzt einen Urlaub leisten, ohne einen Kredit aufzunehmen. Und ich bin überzeugt, dass nachhaltiger Konsum nicht nur gut für die Umwelt ist, sondern auch für das eigene Konto.

In English:

> A year ago I started an experiment: twelve months without new clothes, no new gadgets, no luxury. The reason was simple. Although I have a good income, there was never any money left at the end of the month. I admittedly had no debts, but no savings either.
>
> So I wrote down all my spending. The result shocked me: I was spending almost 200 euros a month on things I didn't need. Often they were bargains. A jumper for 9 euros may be good value, but if you never wear it, it's still wasted money.
>
> At the start it was hard. When my friends went shopping, I went along anyway and didn't buy anything. Now I'm happy to do without. When something breaks, I repair it or buy it second-hand. I compare much more these days: do I really need this? Is there a better quality that lasts longer?
>
> Am I a better person now? No. But I've saved 2,300 euros in one year, and that was worth it. I can now afford a holiday without taking out a loan. And I'm convinced that sustainable consumption isn't only good for the environment but also for your own bank account.

Notes: *übrig* = left over; *aufschreiben* = to write down; *inzwischen* = by now, these days; *gebraucht* = second-hand (the participle of *brauchen* used as an adjective). *die Dinge, die ich nicht gebraucht habe* is a relative clause (A2). *ohne einen Kredit aufzunehmen* (without taking out a loan) and *nicht nur … sondern auch* are previews of lessons 7 and 9. Find the concessions in the text: one *obwohl*, two *zwar … aber*, two *trotzdem*.

## Pronunciation

- *obwohl*: stress on the second syllable, ob-WOHL, with a long *o*.
- *trotzdem*: stress on the first syllable, TROTZ-dem. (When it's a heavy "nevertheless", some speakers stress *-dem*.)
- *zwar*: the *z* is *ts*, so it sounds like "tsvahr".
- *Konsum*: kon-ZOOM, stress at the end; *Luxus*: LUK-sus, short *u*.
- *Schulden*: the *u* is short; *Steuer* rhymes with *teuer*.

## Common mistakes

- Main-clause order after *obwohl*: ~~obwohl ich habe wenig Geld~~ → *obwohl ich wenig Geld habe*.
- Using *trotzdem* like *obwohl*: ~~Trotzdem es teuer war, habe ich es gekauft.~~ → *Obwohl es teuer war, habe ich es gekauft.* Or: *Es war teuer. Trotzdem habe ich es gekauft.*
- Subject before the verb after *trotzdem*: ~~Trotzdem ich habe es gekauft.~~ → *Trotzdem habe ich es gekauft.*
- Confusing *obwohl* and *weil*: ~~Ich spare, obwohl ich ein Auto kaufen will.~~ The saving is *because of* the plan: *weil ich ein Auto kaufen will*.
- *zwar* without *aber*: ~~Das ist zwar teuer.~~ on its own sounds unfinished.
- *sich leisten* with the accusative pronoun: ~~Ich kann mich das nicht leisten.~~ → *Ich kann mir das nicht leisten.* The thing is the accusative object, so the pronoun is dative.
- *ausgeben* for *spend time*: German spends time with *verbringen*: *Ich verbringe viel Zeit im Internet*, but *Ich gebe viel Geld aus*.

## Key points

- *obwohl* + verb at the end gives a fact that does not stop the main event: *Ich kaufe es, obwohl es teuer ist.*
- *trotzdem* is the adverb partner: position 1, verb straight after: *Es ist teuer. Trotzdem kaufe ich es.*
- *weil / deshalb* = expected result; *obwohl / trotzdem* = unexpected result.
- *zwar … aber* concedes a point and then answers it: *Das ist zwar teuer, aber gut.*
- *trotz* + noun is the preposition (lesson 14); *dennoch* and *jedoch* are formal synonyms.
- *Geld ausgeben für*, *sich etwas leisten* (dative pronoun), *auf etwas verzichten*, *Das lohnt sich.*

The words from this lesson are listed below; they join your vocabulary reviews when you complete the lesson.

lessons.title: Goals: um … zu, damit, ohne … zu, statt … zu
lessons.body:
## What this lesson is for

In lesson 6 you linked facts that clash (*obwohl, trotzdem*). This lesson is about goals: why someone does something, what they want to achieve. English says *I'm learning German to work in Vienna* or *so that my children understand their grandparents*. German has two tools for this, *um … zu* and *damit*, and the choice between them depends on one simple question: who is doing it? Then come two more infinitive patterns that work just like *um … zu*: *ohne … zu* (without doing) and *statt … zu* (instead of doing). Finally, *brauchen nicht … zu*, the everyday way to say "you don't have to".

The theme is studying: universities, courses, internships and the skills you need to get a place.

## Review: zu + infinitive

In A2 you learned the infinitive clause: *Ich habe keine Zeit, den Text zu lesen. Ich habe vor, mich zu bewerben.* Remember the rules, because everything in this lesson builds on them:

- *zu* + infinitive goes at the very end of the clause.
- With separable verbs, *zu* goes inside: *anzumelden, einzuschreiben, mitzukommen*.
- The infinitive clause has no subject of its own; the doer is the subject of the main clause.
- A comma usually separates it from the main clause.

## um … zu: in order to

A **[[purpose clause]]** says what an action is for. It answers *Wozu?* (What for?) or *Warum?* When the person who acts and the person who has the goal are the same, use *um … zu*: *um* at the start of the clause, *zu* + infinitive at the end, everything else in between.

| main clause | , | *um* | middle | *zu* + infinitive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| *Ich lerne Deutsch* | , | *um* | *in Wien* | *zu arbeiten.* |
| *Sie jobbt in der Mensa* | , | *um* | *ihr Studium* | *zu finanzieren.* |
| *Er geht in die Bibliothek* | , | *um* | *in Ruhe* | *zu lernen.* |
| *Wir fahren früh los* | , | *um* | *pünktlich zur Vorlesung* | *zu kommen.* |
| *Du musst dich bis Juli einschreiben* | , | *um* | *im Oktober* | *anzufangen.* |

English uses a plain "to" here (*I'm learning German to work in Vienna*), so learners often forget *um*. In German, a purpose needs *um*: ~~Ich lerne Deutsch, in Wien zu arbeiten~~ is wrong.

The *um … zu* clause can also come first. It then takes position 1 and the main verb follows straight after the comma:

- *Um ein Stipendium zu bekommen, braucht man sehr gute Noten.* — To get a scholarship, you need very good grades.
- *Um Geld zu sparen, wohnen viele Studierende in einer WG.* — To save money, many students live in a flat-share.

## damit: so that

When the goal belongs to someone else, you can't use *um … zu*, because the infinitive has no subject to show who that other person is. Use *damit* with a full clause, verb at the end, like *weil*:

- *Ich erkläre es dir noch einmal, damit du es verstehst.* — I'll explain it to you again so that you understand it.
- *Die Uni bietet Kurse an, damit die Studierenden ihr Deutsch verbessern können.* — The university offers courses so that the students can improve their German.
- *Der Professor spricht langsam, damit alle mitschreiben können.* — The professor speaks slowly so that everyone can take notes.

The test is the subject:
